The snout-vent length at metamorphosis in Dermatonotus muelleri reaches 1.88 centimeters , representing the size at which individuals complete their aquatic larval phase and transition to a terrestrial existence. Female ultimate snout-vent length attains 8 centimeters [Li = 8 centimeters], a value derived from long-term field studies of adult cohorts, while males reach a somewhat smaller maximum snout-vent length of 7.2 centimeters [Li = 7.2 centimeters], reflecting a moderate but consistent sexual size dimorphism. This disparity in adult size is paired with corresponding differences in mass, as the ultimate wet weight for females is recorded at 57.1 grams [Wwi = 57.1 grams], whereas males achieve a terminal body mass of 35.1 grams [Wwi = 35.1 grams]. The larger body size of females is a common pattern among burrowing frogs and is hypothesized to be linked to fecundity selection, given that larger females can accommodate greater clutch volumes.

At a constant temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], the period between metamorphosis and the attainment of sexual maturity spans 730 days [tp = 730 days] for both sexes, although the body sizes at which puberty is reached differ. Females become reproductively mature upon reaching a snout-vent length of 7 centimeters [Lp = 7 centimeters], which corresponds to a wet weight at puberty of 38.25 grams [Wwp = 38.25 grams]. Males, in contrast, achieve puberty at a snout-vent length of 6.6 centimeters [Lp = 6.6 centimeters], with a corresponding wet weight at puberty of 27 grams [Wwp = 27 grams]. These values indicate that individuals must accumulate substantial somatic mass before the onset of gonadal activity, a pattern that may reflect the energetic demands of the dry-season breeding strategy typical of this species.

Reproductive output in Dermatonotus muelleri is measured under captive conditions at 25 °C [T = 25 °C] and reveals a daily egg production rate of approximately 29 eggs [Ri = approximately 29 eggs], a remarkably high fecundity for a microhylid frog of its body size. To place this observation in a more accessible biological context, females lay clutches containing approximately 29 eggs [N_R_i = approximately 29 eggs] per spawning event, and these events occur with a frequency of roughly 12 times per year [F_R_i = roughly 12 times per year], effectively representing continuous reproduction under optimal thermal conditions. This sustained laying capacity is among the highest recorded for any neotropical anuran and suggests that females are capable of nearly constant vitellogenesis when food resources and ambient temperatures are favorable.

Eggs of Dermatonotus muelleri are small and yolk-rich, with an average diameter of 1.36 millimeters. From this egg size, the calculated wet weight at birth is 0.0013 grams [Wwb = 0.0013 grams], a minute mass that reflects the substantial post-ovulatory investment in yolk provisioning relative to the overall egg volume. At the opposite end of the life cycle, maximum recorded longevity under controlled laboratory conditions at 25 °C [T = 25 °C] reaches 1825 days [am = 1825 days]. This lifespan is relatively extended for a small-bodied microhylid and may be associated with its fossorial lifestyle, which reduces exposure to predators and environmental extremes.

The protracted developmental period observed in this species is further illustrated by comparing the size at metamorphosis with the sizes required for reproductive maturity. The juvenile cohort begins terrestrial life at a snout-vent length of 1.88 centimeters  and must more than triple in length to reach the female pubertal threshold of 7 centimeters [Lp = 7 centimeters] or the male pubertal threshold of 6.6 centimeters [Lp = 6.6 centimeters]. The time required to bridge this size gap is substantial, with both sexes requiring 730 days following metamorphosis [tp = 730 days following metamorphosis] to achieve sexual maturity at 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. This two-year delay before puberty suggests that Dermatonotus muelleri prioritizes somatic growth and resource accumulation over early breeding, a life-history strategy that is common in environments where adult survival is high but juvenile recruitment is unpredictable.
